previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Meléndez, a man with dilated cardiomyopathy, chronic systolic heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and a history of heavy alcohol use, was admitted after being punched in the chest and reporting his implantable defibrillator had fired. Device interrogation showed no shocks were delivered. He was intoxicated with an ethanol level of 313 and exhibited signs of alcohol withdrawal, managed with diazepam and supportive vitamins. His persistent tachycardia was controlled with metoprolol, and elevated liver enzymes and lipase normalized with supportive care. He reported chronic nausea and vomiting, likely related to alcohol and possible opioid use, and expressed a strong desire for rehabilitation. He stabilized, withdrawal symptoms resolved, and he was discharged to an extended care facility for alcohol treatment with updated medications and follow-up plans.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ with h/o dilated CM, systolic CHF, STEMI s/p cardiac 
catherization, s/p ICD, A-fib on pradaxa, PE, and chronic EtOH 
abuse who presented with abdominal pain and hematemesis.  

# Abdominal pain/hematemesis: Likely due to gastritis and 
possible ___ tear in the setting of vomiting.  Prior 
EGD in ___ showed gastritis and duodenitis.  There was a 
concern for mesenteric ischemia initially, given his rise in 
lactate 3.8 -> 7.8 on the day of admission, but CTA abdomen 
showed patent vasculature and showed no evidence of ischemia. 
The next day, lactate returned to 1.5. Patient was hydrated with 
IV fluids.  He was also started on pantoprazole 40 mg IV Q12H as 
well as ondansetron and promethazine for nausea.  His Hct 
remained stable, and he did not require transfusion.  He also 
remained hemodynamically stable.  Pain was controlled with 
acetaminophen and morphine. His initially mildly elevated AST 
and ALT returned to baseline. Diet was slowly advanced as 
tolerated to regular, without recurrent nausea or abdominal 
pain. He was discharged afebrile, with stable heart rate and 
blood pressure, and minimal abdominal pain.   Was switched to 
oral PPI prior to discharge.  
  
# Chest pain: Patient has extensive history of cardiac disease, 
including dilated cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction 25%), prior 
STEMI, atrial fibrillation, and hypertension. On the day of 
admission, he complained of chest pain. His EKG and troponins, 
however, were within normal limits.  Chest pain resolved prior 
to discharge.   

# EtOH Abuse: Serum EtOH level 283 on admission. Patient was 
given multivitamins, folate, and thiamine and started on CIWA 
scale while in the hospital. He did not have any signs of 
withdrawal during his hospital course.

# Atrial fibrillation: Prior to admission, he was on dabigatran 
for anticoagulation.  Was switched to a heparin drip while in 
the hospital, but transitioned back to dabigatran prior to 
discharge. 

# Dilated cardiomyopathy/sCHF: Patient appeared euvolemic during 
his hospital stay.  Has previously been on furosemide, but had 
not taken it recently as he ran out.  Did not restart given he 
appeared euvolemic.  Restarted metoprolol, losartan.  

# HTN: Patient normotensive to slightly hypertensive.  Had run 
out of many of his home medications prior to discharge, 
including furosemide, lorsartan, and metoprolol.  Restarted 
losartan and metoprolol prior to discharge, but did not restart 
furosemide as above.  Will need BP check and chem-7 checked in 
PCP ___.  

# GERD: Continued PPI, though increased dose in setting of 
hematemesis.

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  Alcohol abuse, severe abdominal pain, hematemesis, rising lactate. 
3.8 x 7.8 despite IV fluids.  Evaluate for mesenteric ischemia.

TECHNIQUE:  Contiguous helical MDCT images were obtained through the abdomen
and pelvis first without IV contrast and then after administration of 150 cc
of Omnipaque IV contrast with arterial and portal venous phase scans. 
Multiplanar axial, coronal, sagittal images were generated.

Total body DLP:  1697.78.

COMPARISON:  Multiple prior CTs of the abdomen and pelvis including ___ at ___.

FINDINGS:

The lung bases are clear.  There is a single pacemaker lead in the heart. 
There is no pericardial effusion.

CT ABDOMEN WITH CONTRAST:  The liver is diffusely hypoattenuating suggesting
fatty infiltration.  There are no concerning liver lesions or intrahepatic
biliary dilation.  A 0.6 cm hypodensity in the right lobe of the liver
(4b:254) is unchanged.  The gallbladder is unremarkable without stones.  The
spleen, pancreas, adrenal glands are within normal limits.  The kidneys
present symmetric nephrograms and excretion of contrast.  A peripheral
hypodensity in the left kidney is stable since ___, likely scarring
from prior infection.  The ureters are normal throughout their visualized
course.  There is no hydronephrosis.

The stomach, small and large bowel are within normal limits without evidence
of obstruction.  There is no ascites, free air or abdominal wall hernias. 
There is no mesenteric or retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy.

CTA ABDOMEN:  The major abdominal vessels are patent including the celiac
axis, SMA, and ___.  The aorta and branch iliac vessels are of normal caliber.
There is a duplicated left renal artery (4a:67).  Motion artifact somewhat
limits evaluation of the venous structures however there is patency of the
portal, splenic and superior mesenteric veins.  There is no evidence of
vasculitis or other vascular abnormality.  

CT PELVIS WITH CONTRAST:  The urinary bladder, prostate, seminal vesicles, and
rectum are unremarkable.  There are scattered phleboliths.  There is no free
fluid or lymphadenopathy in the pelvis.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:  There are no concerning blastic or lytic lesions.  There
are mild degenerative changes in the thoracolumbar spine most severe at L5-S1
with end plate sclerosis, disc height loss, and disc vacuum phenomenon.  There
is slight scoliosis.

IMPRESSION:
1. Patent abdominal vasculature without findings to suggest mesenteric
ischemia.  Normal-appearing bowel.

2. Peripheral hypodensity in the left kidney stable since ___ is likely
sequela of prior infection.

3. Fatty liver.
